property.name: Pages
property.value: A board nailed to the gatepost, the paint gone grey. "ASHWOLD. Bridge toll one copper the cart, free the foot. Delvers: the road up is the north road. The Rest has beds. Pay the smith before he starts, not after."

property.name: Pages
property.value: Bills nailed one over another. The top one is fresh: "WANTED, word of the party of four that went up on the feast day and has not come down. Their gear was carried on a grey mule. Any word to the Rest." Beneath it, older and softer with rain, is another notice in the same hand. And beneath that, another.␟The notice had been written three times before this one. The first had been taken down by rain before the week was out. The second lasted until the wind split it from top to bottom. This third sheet had been copied with greater care than either before it, each letter pressed firmly into the paper as though the hand that held the quill believed neatness might succeed where hope already had begun to fail. It hung upon the board with four long nails driven through the corners, fixed above older notices written in the same careful hand, their edges grey with weather and curled so tightly they had become part of the timber itself.␟To every traveller, hunter, charcoal burner, forester, peddler, shepherd, miner, and all others who pass between Ashwold, the Whispering Wood, and the Deepdelve: if these words find your eyes before winter finds the road, I ask only that you remember four honest folk who climbed the mountain upon the Feast Day and have not since returned. They departed after the bells had finished their morning ringing, carrying enough provisions for six days and no more. A grey mule bore the greater weight of their burden. The beast answers to the name Ash, though it is gentle enough to follow any hand that offers grain.␟Those sought are these: Brann, a broad man with a scar laid white across the bridge of his nose — his left leg has troubled him since a timber fell upon it many winters ago, and he walks with a slight favour whenever rain is near. Elske, who wears a red wool scarf knitted by her mother before the old woman lost the use of her hands; she is not known to leave home without it, no matter the season. Toman, once a smith of this village, whose beard carries more ash and filings than black, no matter how often he washes. Harl, youngest among them, scarcely grown into the beard he keeps trying to grow, with an unfortunate habit of whistling whenever silence grows too long.␟Should they be found alive, may whatever business delayed them be forgiven, and may they be guided safely home. Should they be found dead, I ask only that someone tell us where they lie — stone may keep its dead if it must, but mothers and wives should not be left wondering which hillside to mourn. If only their belongings are found, bring word before anything is disturbed. The mule returned alone two mornings after the Feast Day. Its packs were still tied. Nothing had been taken; nothing had been added. It stood before the mill until dusk without touching the bucket set before it, and whenever anyone reached for the straps it turned its head toward the mountain — not once, but again and again, as though expecting voices that never followed.␟There is little coin in Ashwold, and less to spare. No reward worthy of the labour can be promised. Still, whoever brings true word of the Four shall always find a place beside my hearth, bread while I have flour enough to bake it, and gratitude that neither weather nor years shall wear away. Leave any account with Old Mera at the mill, or fasten your own notice beneath this one, that no traveller need carry the burden farther than the next village. Do not remove this notice. Another pair of eyes may yet read what yours already have. — Written on behalf of the families of the Four.␟By the time the forester brought down his ledger from the tally-platform, the leaves had already begun to yellow along the edge of the Whispering Wood. The miner carried the chalk board from the abandoned cart beneath his arm, careful not to brush away what little the rain had spared, and Old Mera wrapped the unfinished letter in clean linen before placing it upon her kitchen table. Last of all came the rubbing taken from the cave wall, charcoal worked carefully over thin paper until every cut of the chisel stood black against the page. There was little enough to show for the journey of four honest folk, yet the village gathered around those few scraps as though they had been relics from saints.␟No one suggested another search. Not because the people of Ashwold lacked courage, but because every man who had climbed beyond the first chamber returned with the same account. The bedrolls remained where they had been laid. The cook pot still waited beside cold ash. The letter never moved from beneath the cup. Beyond the narrow passage the air grew colder, the lamp burned strangely, and before long each search party found itself standing once again at the entrance without recalling how it had turned back. Some remembered hearing footsteps. Others swore they heard nothing at all. None reached the place where the final words had been scratched into the stone.␟Winter came early that year. Snow gathered along the roofs before the last of the barley had been threshed, and the notice upon the village board curled at its corners beneath frost and rain. Travellers paused to read it before continuing north or south. Some nodded quietly. Others crossed themselves before the mountain road disappeared amongst the pines. A few added rumours of their own beneath it, though Mera removed those before another sunrise. She would allow no man to burden the families with stories dressed as truth. The grey mule lived out the remainder of its years in Ashwold. No one thought to sell it. Children carried sacks of grain upon its back from the mill to the baker's yard, and in summer it drew the small cart used to fetch water from the lower spring. It remained as gentle as ever, yet whenever someone tried to lead it toward the mountain track it planted its feet upon the earth exactly as it had before the cave, lowered its head, and would go no farther. The oldest folk in the village ceased calling it stubborn after the first few attempts.␟When another Feast Day returned, Mera climbed upon the bench before the notice board and drew the paper loose herself. The nails came reluctantly, taking splinters of the old timber with them. She folded the sheet with slow hands, once for each of the four whose names were written there, and placed it beside the forester's ledger, the miner's account, and the unfinished letter inside the mill chest where damp could not reach them. The space upon the board remained empty. Not because there was nothing left to say — because every soul in Ashwold already knew the words by heart, and there was no hand among them willing to write another notice over the place where the first one had waited so long.

property.name: Pages
property.value: The village well, the rope worn into a groove on the stone lip. Somebody has scratched a tally into the coping — five short strokes, then five, then five, and one. Nobody in Ashwold will tell you what is being counted.

property.name: Pages
property.value: A pillar of pale stone with the Holy Light's mark cut into it, and the cut kept clean of moss by hands that come often. Offerings at its foot: a child's carved bird, a pick head, three copper coins, and a woman's ring with the stone gone. "GO UP IN THE LIGHT. COME DOWN IN IT."

property.name: Pages
property.value: Seven stones, and only two of them old. The new ones are not weathered enough to read from a distance, so you have to stand close. Every one of them gives the same year. Three give the same month.

property.name: Pages
property.value: Flat stones set into the brook, worn smooth in a line — and worn most in the middle, where the mules go. On the far bank the mud holds prints going north. You count them out of habit. Far more go up than come back.

property.name: Pages
property.value: The wheel turns slow and the leat runs clean, which means somebody clears it. Sacks are stacked under the eave and tallied in chalk on the door: flour for the Rest, flour for the camp, flour for the mine. The mine's column has not been added to in three weeks.

property.name: Pages
property.value: A stone older than the village, half sunk and furred with lichen. The letters on it are not the ones anyone here uses now, and the one word that can still be made out is a name — Ychellen. The fields stop at it. Nobody has ever ploughed past it, and nobody can say why not.

property.name: Pages
property.value: A carrier's wagon with a wheel off and the axle propped on a stone. The load has been taken, but not hurriedly: the ropes are coiled, not cut. Whoever it was walked on east, and meant to come back for it.
